title: How Many Boxes of 12x24 Tile for a 10x10 Floor?
description: A 10x10 floor with 16 sq ft boxes of 12x24 tile needs 7 boxes, including 10% extra for cuts. See the steps and why large tiles may need more.

body.text: For a 10x10 floor tiled with 12x24 tile that covers 16 sq ft per box, you need 7 boxes. That number already includes 10% extra for cuts and breakage. You can plug in your own room size and box coverage in the [Tile Calculator](/tile-calculator) to get the answer for your project.
The worked example, step by step
Here is how the calculator gets to 7 boxes for a 10x10 floor:

items: Find the floor area: 10 ft x 10 ft = 100 sq ft.
Add the 10% extra for cuts and breakage. That brings the tile you need to 110 sq ft.
Divide by the coverage printed on the box. With 16 sq ft per box, 110 sq ft divided by 16 sq ft per box comes out to a bit under 7 boxes.
Round up to whole boxes. You can't buy part of a box, so you buy 7 boxes.

body.text: The key point is the rounding. Always round up, never down. Running short by even a few tiles means a second trip, and a later purchase may come from a different dye lot with a slightly different shade.
Check the coverage on your box

The 16 sq ft per box figure is only an example. Coverage per box varies by brand, thickness and tile line, so the square footage on your label may be quite different. Read the coverage printed on the box or in the product listing, then use that number in the calculator. If your box covers less than 16 sq ft, you will need more boxes. If it covers more, you may need fewer.
Why large tiles can need more extra in a small room

The 10% extra is the common starting point for cuts and breakage, and it is what the calculator uses in the example above. For a deeper look at when to go higher, see our guide on [how much overage for tile cuts and waste](/blog/how-much-overage-for-tile-cuts-and-waste).
Large tiles like 12x24 can call for a higher percentage in a small room, for a few reasons:

items: Each cut wastes more. When a tile is 24 inches long, trimming it to fit along a wall can leave an offcut too short or awkward to reuse elsewhere.
There are fewer tiles overall. In a small floor, a few ruined pieces take up a bigger share of your total than they would in a large room.
Pattern choices add waste. A straight lay uses the least. A diagonal layout or a brick-style offset creates more angled and trimmed pieces.
Odd room shapes add cuts. Alcoves, closets, doorways and corners all produce extra trimming.

body.text: If your layout is diagonal, your room has several jogs, or you are new to cutting tile, try a higher extra percentage in the calculator and see how the box count changes. A 10x10 room is small enough that one or two broken tiles matter. The right percentage for your layout is a judgment call, so the 10% in this example is a starting point, not a guarantee.
Why a spare box can be worth it

Even if the math lands close to a whole number, a little extra margin is a reasonable safeguard. Leftover tile is useful later for repairs, since a cracked tile years down the road is much easier to swap if you still have matching pieces from the same lot. Check the store's return policy before you buy, and keep unopened boxes if returns are allowed.
Quick tips before you order

items: Measure the actual floor, not the room's outer dimensions. If the room isn't a perfect rectangle, break it into sections. Our post on [how to calculate square footage of a room](/blog/how-to-calculate-square-footage-of-a-room) walks through it.
Don't subtract for cabinets or a tub unless they are permanent and you are certain no tile goes under them.
Buy all your boxes at once so the shade and dye lot match.
Use the coverage per box printed on the label, since it already accounts for the tile's true size.

body.text: If you are tiling a smaller space, like a bathroom, see [how much tile for a 5x8 bathroom](/blog/how-much-tile-for-5x8-bathroom) for another example.
FAQ
Do I need to buy extra if I'm using 12x24 tile?
Yes. The calculator adds 10% extra for cuts and breakage. Large tiles waste more per cut, so in a small room or with a diagonal pattern you may want to raise that percentage in the calculator.
What if my box covers a different number of square feet?
Use the coverage printed on your box. The 16 sq ft per box in this example is just one possibility. Enter your real number in the [Tile Calculator](/tile-calculator) and the box count will adjust.
Should I round down if I'm only a little over a box?
No. Always round up to the next whole box. If you come up short, you have to reorder, and later boxes may not match in color.
Does the layout pattern change how many boxes I need?
It can. A straight lay wastes the least, while diagonal or offset patterns create more cut pieces. If you plan anything other than a straight lay, raise the extra percentage before ordering.
